title: Superconducting gap: magnitude, nodes and phase
summary: Read gap measurements with their probe and model. Distinguish an excitation scale from evidence for nodes, relative sign or bulk superconductivity.

review.scope: Edited pinned A5 chapter, selected BCS/Choi and phase-sensitive primary passages, review passages, Hardy/Carbotte abstracts and an independent ideal-DOS state-counting check. Selected Fischer tunneling, Dressel optical review and Seibold disordered-response author-version passages; identified manuscript dates retained. Selected Sheet and Kumar point-contact author passages, with publisher abstracts checked separately. Selected Damascelli, Wang, Prozorov-Giannetta and Shakeripour author-version methods and interpretation passages mapped to the remaining probe controls.
limitations: Selected source checks do not constitute full scientific validation or independent experimental replication.
Hardy is abstract-scoped; tricrystal image fits, uncertainties and all underlying review citations were not independently reproduced.
No sample-specific gap amplitude or transition temperature was re-extracted; calculated gaps are not experimental records.
The DOS check assumes a clean isotropic constant-DOS mean-field model, not a universal tunneling spectrum.

All seven listed probe rows have selected source support, but the table is an editorial methods map, not an exhaustive protocol or certified dataset. Full final-version comparisons, underlying experimental data and independent review remain open.

claims.statement: A superconducting gap is an energy scale in a specified excitation spectrum. Its magnitude, momentum dependence and relative phase answer different questions. A suppression of spectral weight is not automatically a superconducting gap, and a fitted gap does not automatically define the temperature of bulk superconductivity. This entry organizes observations and model assumptions rather than ranking materials by a single gap ratio.

claims.statement: In this magnitude-only model, replacing a gap by its negative leaves the excitation energies unchanged. Likewise, independently summing two uncoupled spectral contributions cannot recover their relative sign. This is a limited counterexample to inferring phase from a gap magnitude; it does not say that every interference-sensitive spectrum is phase blind.

claims.statement: A tunnel conductance resembles the sample density of states only under counterelectrode and matrix-element assumptions; the selected Fischer review gives the thermal convolution and explains the resolution role of lock-in modulation. Do not identify every conductance peak with $\Delta$. Optical interpretation also depends on scattering and multiband weights: the selected Dressel review compares competing fits, while Seibold and colleagues distinguish DOS peaks, excitation thresholds and collective absorption within a disordered model. These are source-scoped cautions, not a new fit to any specimen. Photoemission and thermodynamic probes constrain other aspects; magnitude-sensitive measurements alone do not determine relative phase.

claims.statement: Hardy and colleagues report a strong linear term in the penetration-depth change of YBa2Cu3O6.95 single crystals over approximately 3–25 K using a 900 MHz resonator. This is evidence relevant to low-energy excitations under their sample conditions, not a direct measurement of gap phase. The present check covers the publisher abstract.

claims.statement: By contrast, Tsuei and Kirtley use scanning SQUID measurements of NCCO/PCCO tricrystals to test phase-sensitive predictions. Their designed frustrated geometry produces a half-flux signal, while two unfrustrated NCCO geometries serve as controls. The inference depends on junction geometry and the associated model, not merely on observing a spectral dip. Selected author-manuscript passages and the control description were checked; the image fits were not independently reproduced.

claims.statement: Nodes, relative sign and topology are distinct. A low-temperature power law can constrain low-energy excitations without uniquely selecting a pairing representation. A fully open gap on each Fermi-surface sheet can coexist with a relative sign change between sheets. Disorder and sample inhomogeneity must be considered before translating a temperature dependence into a symmetry assignment.

claims.statement: A zero-bias feature alone is not a unique topology test. Identify its field, temperature, position and junction dependence, then compare explicit alternative models. Likewise, a spectroscopic gap-closing temperature must not silently replace a resistive or thermodynamic $T_c$ in a gap ratio. These are inference and reporting limits, not a claim that one alternative explains every observed feature.

claims.statement: For point contacts, a barrier model is only part of the interpretation. Sheet and colleagues distinguish dissipative thermal contacts from a diffusive regime without significant local heating; non-ballistic does not always mean thermal. Kumar and Sheet show how multiple constrictions can mix responses in a network model. These examples motivate contact controls; they neither diagnose every observed peak nor prove that every unconventional spectrum is an artifact.
claims.conditions: Contact geometry, elastic and inelastic mean free paths, barrier model and sample-specific spectrum; network examples are not a universal diagnosis.

claims.derivationNote: Source-specific contact regimes and model constructions support the cautions; their combination as reporting guidance is editorial, not a proof about every experimental spectrum.

claims.statement: The measured ARPES intensity includes occupation and matrix-element factors, and quantitative analysis also requires resolution and background treatment. A leading-edge displacement therefore needs a model before it is reported as a gap amplitude. For calorimetry, Wang and colleagues separately measure addenda and discuss impurity contributions, normalization and thermal equilibration in their MgB2 sample. Heat capacity is measured; entropy requires an integration and reference choice. [R12](#ref-source-d679e3d02f15050c) [R13](#ref-source-18085282135e3fe4)

claims.statement: Penetration depth and heat transport require different controls. The Prozorov-Giannetta review discusses geometry, nonlocality and magnetic or surface contributions, including competing interpretations of a power law. Shakeripour and colleagues warn that nonsuperconducting regions can contribute to a residual heat-conduction term and that multiband response can obscure a particular gap. These selected methodological cautions do not import the reviews' historical material-symmetry assignments as current verdicts. [R14](#ref-source-35bdae325860140f) [R15](#ref-source-63de87eb1fb70b58)
